title: Design a Text Editor
description: Brute force to optimized: a single string with cursor-index slicing versus two stacks split at the cursor, both edited only at their tops.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a text editor with a cursor. Implement addText(text) (append text at the cursor), deletePrevChars(k) (delete up to k characters just before the cursor, returning the actual number deleted), cursorLeft(k) (move the cursor left up to k positions) and cursorRight(k) (move the cursor right up to k positions), both returning the last min(10, current text length before the cursor) characters immediately before the cursor after moving.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Cursor splits text into a before-part and after-part, with movement and edits both near the cursor\"","The classic two-stack (or gap buffer) text editor technique"],["Edits (add/delete) only ever happen right at the cursor","Both stacks only need push/pop at their tops, never arbitrary-position insertion"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

The cursor divides the current text into everything before it and everything after it. addText inserts right at the cursor (extending the before-part), deletePrevChars removes from just before the cursor, and cursorLeft/cursorRight shift characters across the cursor boundary in one direction or the other.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Piles of Cards Representing Text Before and After a Cursor
blocks.text: Picture the text as two piles of cards placed face up: one pile holding everything BEFORE the cursor (read bottom to top, left to right), and one holding everything AFTER (read top to bottom for correct left-to-right order). Typing adds a card to the top of the "before" pile; moving the cursor moves cards, one at a time, from the top of one pile to the top of the other.

blocks.caption: A left stack (before cursor) and a right stack (after cursor), both edited only at their tops

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: addText("leetcode"), deletePrevChars(4), addText("practice"), cursorRight(3), cursorLeft(8), deletePrevChars(10), cursorLeft(2), cursorRight(6)
5. How Should We Think?

Before representing the text as one long string with cursor-index-based slicing (which requires O(n) shifting for every edit), notice that maintaining TWO separate stacks, one for everything before the cursor and one for everything after, lets every operation touch only the very TOP of one stack at a time, since the cursor only ever interacts with characters immediately adjacent to it.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: addText always inserts right where the cursor is, which is exactly the top of the "before cursor" stack, an O(1) push per character.

Observation 2: deletePrevChars removes characters immediately before the cursor, exactly the top of the "before cursor" stack, an O(1) pop per character removed.

Observation 3: cursorLeft(k) moves the cursor left, which means characters that were just before the cursor are now just after it, so popping from the left stack and pushing onto the right stack, one at a time, correctly simulates this movement.

Observation 4: cursorRight(k) is symmetric, popping from the right stack and pushing onto the left stack. After any cursor movement, the required "up to 10 characters before the cursor" is simply the top (up to) 10 elements of the left stack, read in the correct order.

This leads to two stacks, left (characters before the cursor) and right (characters after), with addText/deletePrevChars only touching the left stack's top, and cursorLeft/cursorRight moving characters one at a time between the two stacks' tops.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain the text as a single string, with a separate cursor index. Every operation directly manipulates the string via slicing/concatenation.
Step by step algorithm

items: addText(text): insert text into the string at the cursor index, and advance the cursor by text's length.
deletePrevChars(k): remove up to k characters from the string just before the cursor index, adjusting the cursor accordingly.
cursorLeft(k)/cursorRight(k): adjust the cursor index directly (clamped to valid bounds), then slice out the last 10 characters before the new cursor position.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A single string with a cursor index directly models the editor's state, easy to reason about.
Every insert or delete requires shifting all characters after the cursor, an O(n) cost per call, too slow for up to 4*10^5 total characters across 2*10^4 calls.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per addText/deletePrevChars call (shifting), O(1) plus O(10) per cursor move (aside from the O(n) shift needed if using a plain string's cursor tracking naively; some implementations avoid the shift for pure moves but string-based inserts/deletes remain O(n)).
Space: O(n) for the string.

Limitation: since edits only ever happen right at the cursor, representing the text as two separate stacks (one per side of the cursor) turns every edit and cursor move into an O(1)-per-character operation, with no shifting required.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why string shifting is unnecessary: addText and deletePrevChars ALWAYS operate right at the cursor position, never anywhere else, so there is no need for a data structure supporting arbitrary-position insertion/deletion.

The two-stack design: represent everything before the cursor as a stack (top = character immediately before the cursor) and everything after as another stack (top = character immediately after the cursor).

Why cursor movement becomes O(1) per character: moving the cursor left by one position means the character just before it becomes the character just after it, exactly a pop from the left stack followed by a push onto the right stack (and the symmetric operation for moving right).

The core idea: two stacks, edited only at their tops, directly modeling "everything before" and "everything after" the cursor, giving O(1) amortized cost per character for every operation.

Maintain a left stack (before cursor) and a right stack (after cursor). addText pushes each character onto the left stack. deletePrevChars pops from the left stack. cursorLeft/cursorRight move characters between the two stacks' tops, one at a time. Both cursor moves return the top (up to) 10 characters of the left stack, in order.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for addText("leetcode"), deletePrevChars(4), addText("practice")

blocks.caption: Two stacks, edited only at their tops, give O(1) amortized cost per operation

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since every operation (typing, deleting, or moving the cursor) only ever interacts with characters immediately adjacent to the cursor, representing the text as two stacks split at the cursor means every such interaction only ever touches the TOP of one stack, an O(1) operation. Moving the cursor by k positions correctly transfers exactly k characters (one at a time) between the two stacks' tops, preserving their correct relative order on each side, since a stack pop-then-push exactly reverses, then re-reverses, the traversal direction appropriately for the two representations.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) amortized per character for addText, deletePrevChars, and cursor moves (each character moves between structures a bounded number of times); O(10) to extract the trailing substring for cursor moves.
Space: O(total text length) for the two stacks combined.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Design a Text Editor is the canonical "two stacks split at a cursor" design problem, exploiting that all edits and moves only ever touch the boundary between the two halves.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to clamp k to the available characters on the relevant side (fewer characters may remain than requested to delete or move over).
Reading the left stack's trailing 10 characters in the wrong order (must read them in original left-to-right text order, not stack-pop order).

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["cursorLeft/cursorRight called with the cursor already at an extreme end","Simply moves as far as possible and stops, returning the trailing characters correctly."],["deletePrevChars(k) with fewer than k characters before the cursor","Deletes only what is available, returning the actual (smaller) count."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "since all edits happen at the cursor, two stacks split there turn every operation into a top-of-stack push/pop" is the key insight that should be stated before coding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "a cursor divides data into a before-part and after-part, with edits near the cursor", think: two stacks split at the cursor, edited only at their tops.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support undo/redo on top of this design?
How would you support inserting or deleting NOT at the cursor, but at an arbitrary position?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The "gap buffer" data structure used in real text editors, a close relative of this two-stack technique.
Any "cursor/pointer splits a sequence into two actively-edited halves" design problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The single-string approach costs O(n) per edit due to shifting; the two-stack approach costs O(1) amortized per character for every operation, both using O(n) total space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: two stacks split at the cursor, one for "before" and one for "after," edited only at their tops.
Core Idea: addText/deletePrevChars only touch the left stack's top; cursor moves transfer characters one at a time between the two stacks' tops.
Time: O(n) per edit for the single-string approach, O(1) amortized per character for the two-stack approach.
Most Important Observation: since all edits and moves happen exactly at the cursor, splitting the text into two stacks there turns every operation into an O(1) top-of-stack access.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, practical design problem modeling real text-editor internals.
One line memory trick: two stacks split at the cursor; moving the cursor pops from one, pushes onto the other.
